query: A radiomics-derived imaging signature from CT imaging can predict high-risk patients with neuroblastoma.

hypothesis.title: Radiomics-derived CT imaging signature predicts high‑risk neuroblastoma patients
hypothesis.population: Children and adolescents diagnosed with neuroblastoma who undergo contrast‑enhanced CT imaging
hypothesis.intervention: Application of a radiomics-derived imaging signature extracted from CT scans
hypothesis.outcome: Accurate prediction of high‑risk disease status (as defined by established clinical risk criteria)
hypothesis.clinical_context: Risk stratification in pediatric neuroblastoma to guide treatment intensity and prognosis

steps.name: Comprehensive Literature Review & Feasibility Assessment
steps.description: Conduct a systematic review of existing radiomics studies in neuroblastoma and other pediatric cancers. Summarize published imaging signatures, feature extraction pipelines, and machine‑learning methods. Evaluate the availability of contrast‑enhanced CT scans, image quality standards, and prior risk‑stratification criteria (INRG, COG). Perform a feasibility analysis to estimate sample size requirements for training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts.

steps.name: Formulation of Study Objectives & Hypothesis
steps.description: Define the primary objective: to develop and validate a CT‑based radiomics signature that predicts high‑risk neuroblastoma status as defined by INRG/COG criteria. Secondary objectives may include assessing prognostic value for event‑free survival, treatment response, and performing decision‑curve analysis for clinical utility.

steps.name: Study Design & Protocol Development
steps.description: Draft a multicenter, retrospective‑prospective diagnostic accuracy study. Specify inclusion criteria (age ≥18 years, histologically confirmed neuroblastoma, baseline contrast‑enhanced CT within 30 days of diagnosis) and exclusion criteria (poor image quality, prior therapy before CT). Outline the two‑phase design: (1) retrospective training/validation using existing scans from 3‑5 academic pediatric oncology centers, and (2) prospective external validation in a separate cohort. Define endpoints, sample‑size calculations (e.g., target AUC ≥ 0.85 with 95 % CI width ≤ 0.10), and statistical analysis plan.

steps.name: Ethics & Regulatory Approvals
steps.description: Prepare Institutional Review Board (IRB) submissions for each participating site, addressing data privacy, de‑identification, and consent (waiver for retrospective data, informed consent for prospective validation). Register the study on ClinicalTrials.gov and comply with GDPR/HIPAA regulations for international data sharing.

steps.name: Site Selection & Investigator Training
steps.description: Identify 4‑6 pediatric oncology centers with high neuroblastoma case volumes and standardized CT protocols. Conduct investigator webinars covering study objectives, inclusion/exclusion criteria, image acquisition parameters, and radiomics workflow. Provide a detailed imaging manual (slice thickness ≥1.5 mm, arterial phase timing, reconstruction kernel) to ensure harmonized data.

steps.name: Data Acquisition & Image Standardization
steps.description: Collect DICOM CT scans from each site. Apply a standardized preprocessing pipeline: (a) DICOM de‑identification, (b) resampling to isotropic voxel size (1 mm³), (c) intensity normalization using tissue‑based calibration (e.g., aortic lumen), (d) artifact correction (metal, motion). Document scanner models, acquisition parameters, and any deviations in a central registry.

steps.name: Clinical Data Collection & Gold‑Standard Risk Assignment
steps.description: Gather clinical variables required for INRG/COG risk classification: age at diagnosis, stage, MYCN amplification, histopathology, serum ferritin, LDH, and Shimada biology. Assign each patient a ‘high‑risk’ or ‘non‑high‑risk’ label based on the officially accepted criteria. Store data in a secure REDCap database linked to imaging identifiers.

steps.name: Radiomics Feature Extraction Pipeline Development
steps.description: Implement a validated, open‑source pipeline (e.g., PyRadiomics) within a containerized environment (Docker). Steps include: (a) semi‑automatic tumor segmentation on portal‑venous phase CT using a consensus protocol, (b) inter‑observer reproducibility assessment (intraclass correlation coefficient >0.80) on a subset, (c) extraction of first‑order statistics, shape descriptors, texture features (GLCM, GLRLM, NGTDM, GLSZM), and wavelet‑filtered features. Store feature matrices in a centralized repository.

steps.name: Feature Selection & Signature Construction (Training Cohort)
steps.description: Perform dimensionality reduction on the training set (≈60 % of retrospective cohort) using: (a) variance thresholding, (b) correlation analysis (remove one of any pair r > 0.9), (c) univariate association with high‑risk status (Benjamini‑Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05), and (d) recursive feature elimination combined with cross‑validated LASSO logistic regression. Derive a parsimonious radiomics signature (≥10 features) weighted by model coefficients.

steps.name: Model Development & Internal Validation
steps.description: Fit a multivariable logistic regression (or alternative machine‑learning classifier such as Random Forest or Gradient Boosting) using the selected radiomics signature. Apply 5‑fold cross‑validation within the training set to tune hyperparameters and assess discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer‑Lemeshow test, calibration plot), and decision‑curve analysis. Record performance metrics with 95 % confidence intervals.

steps.name: External Validation (Retrospective Cohort)
steps.description: Apply the finalized model to the remaining retrospective cohort (≈40 % of original data) from participating sites that were not used for model training. Compute AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative predictive values, and calibration slope. Compare model predictions with gold‑standard risk status to evaluate generalizability.

steps.name: Prospective Validation Cohort
steps.description: Enroll newly diagnosed neuroblastoma patients at participating centers over a 24‑month period. Acquire CT scans following the same standardized protocol, extract radiomics features using the pre‑built pipeline, and generate risk predictions in real time (blinded to treating physicians). After definitive risk assignment by standard clinical criteria, assess model performance prospectively, focusing on time‑to‑prediction, feasibility, and impact on clinical decision‑making.

steps.name: Statistical Analysis & Subgroup Exploration
steps.description: Conduct the predefined statistical analysis plan using R or Python. Primary analysis: comparison of AUC between radiomics model and standard clinical risk factors alone (using DeLong’s test). Secondary analyses: (a) incremental value of adding radiomics to clinical model (net reclassification improvement), (b) performance across imaging platforms (different CT manufacturers), (c) effect of tumor location (retroperitoneal vs. cervical), (d) age sub‑groups (<12 months vs. ≥12 months).

steps.name: Health‑Economic & Clinical Impact Assessment
steps.description: Perform a decision‑analytic modeling study to estimate potential cost‑savings if the radiomics signature enables early identification of high‑risk patients and appropriate escalation of therapy. Use quality‑adjusted life‑year (QALY) estimates and incremental cost‑effectiveness ratios (ICERs) based on published pediatric neuroblastoma treatment costs.

steps.name: Data Management, Quality Assurance, and Monitoring
steps.description: Establish a central data coordinating center responsible for data integrity checks, version control of imaging pipelines, and audit trails. Conduct periodic monitoring visits to each site to verify compliance with imaging standards, segmentation reproducibility, and consent documentation.

steps.name: Manuscript Preparation & Dissemination
steps.description: Draft manuscripts describing (a) the development and validation of the radiomics signature, (b) the prospective validation results, and (c) the health‑economic impact analysis. Submit to high‑impact oncology and radiology journals. Present findings at pediatric oncology conferences (e.g., SIOP, ASCO‑Pediatric). Release the radiomics code and de‑identified feature dataset in a public repository (e.g., GitHub, TCIA) to foster reproducibility.

steps.name: Implementation Planning & Clinical Integration
steps.description: If validation is successful, create a clinical decision‑support tool (web‑based or integrated into PACS) that automatically processes CT scans, computes the radiomics risk score, and presents results alongside standard clinical variables. Pilot the tool in one center, gather user feedback, and develop training modules for radiologists and oncologists before broader roll‑out.

result.evaluation:
**Overall Assessment**

The proposed study is a well‑structured, multistage radiomics project that moves from systematic literature review to prospective clinical validation and health‑economic modelling. As a whole it covers the essential elements of a rigorous diagnostic‑accuracy investigation (design, data acquisition, feature engineering, model development, internal/external validation, regulatory compliance, and dissemination). The plan is largely complete, but several items need clarification, risk mitigation, or additional detail before the work can be considered fully feasible and scientifically robust.

---

## Strengths  

| Domain | Comments |
|--------|----------|
| **Scientific Rationale** | The hypothesis (CT‑based radiomics can predict high‑risk neuroblastoma) is clinically relevant; early risk stratification could influence therapy intensity. |
| **Stepwise Design** | Clear progression from literature review → objectives → protocol → retrospective training/validation → prospective external validation, mirroring the TRIPOD‑AI/ML reporting standards. |
| **Multi‑center Approach** | Inclusion of 3‑5 academic pediatric oncology centres for training and a separate centre for prospective validation improves generalisability and addresses spectrum bias. |
| **Standardised Imaging Protocol** | Explicit slice‑thickness, phase‑timing, and reconstruction‑kernel requirements, plus a central preprocessing pipeline, minimise technical heterogeneity – a common pitfall in paediatric radiomics. |
| **Transparent Feature Pipeline** | Use of an open‑source, containerised PyRadiomics workflow, with reproducibility checks (ICC > 0.80) and version control, satisfies FAIR‑data principles. |
| **Robust Model Development** | Combination of variance filtering, correlation pruning, BH‑adjusted univariate screening, and recursive feature elimination with cross‑validated LASSO is appropriate for high‑dimensional data. |
| **Validation Strategy** | Internal 5‑fold CV, retrospective external validation, followed by a true prospective cohort (real‑time blinded predictions) meets the “three‑phase” validation recommended for AI‑based diagnostics. |
| **Statistical Rigor** | Pre‑specified primary endpoint (AUC ≥ 0.85, CI ≤ 0.10) and detailed secondary analyses (net reclassification, subgroup performance, calibration) are in line with FDA‑MAIA and CONSORT‑AI guidance. |
| **Regulatory & Ethics Plan** | IRB waivers for retrospective data, informed consent for prospective enrolment, GDPR/HIPAA compliance, and trial registration are all addressed. |
| **Health‑Economic Component** | Including a decision‑analytic model (QALY, ICER) strengthens the translational impact and is often required for reimbursement discussions. |
| **Dissemination & Reproducibility** | Commitment to open‑source code, de‑identified feature sets, and presentations at major conferences will facilitate external replication. |
| **Implementation Pathway** | Planning a decision‑support tool and pilot‑testing it before rollout demonstrates foresight toward clinical adoption. |

---

## Weaknesses / Gaps  

| Area | Issue | Potential Impact | Recommendation |
|------|-------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Hypothesis Statement** | The `study_goal` field is left blank (“Investigate the hypothesis: ”). | Lack of a concise, testable hypothesis may hinder protocol approval and downstream reporting. | Draft a one‑sentence hypothesis, e.g., “A CT‑based radiomics signature can discriminate high‑risk from non‑high‑risk neuroblastoma at diagnosis with AUC ≥ 0.85.” |
| **Sample‑Size Justification** | Only a target AUC and CI width are mentioned; no explicit numbers of patients per cohort, nor prevalence assumptions. | Under‑ or over‑powered study; may miss required events for reliable model calibration. | Perform a formal power calculation (e.g., using Obuchowski’s method) based on estimated high‑risk prevalence (~30 % in neuroblastoma) and desired precision for AUC. Provide separate numbers for training, internal validation, retrospective external, and prospective cohorts. |
| **Missing Matched Modules** | Several steps (e.g., literature review, ethics, site training, health‑economic analysis) have `matched_module: null`. | May limit automation/traceability if the platform expects module linkage. | Either map these activities to existing modules (e.g., `StudyDesignModule`, `EconomicAnalysisModule`) or create custom wrappers to ensure all steps are tracked in the workflow system. |
| **Segmentation Process** | “Semi‑automatic tumor segmentation” is described, but no specific software, algorithm, or inter‑observer protocol is detailed. | Variability in ROI definition could dominate model performance; reproducibility concerns. | Choose a specific segmentation tool (e.g., 3D Slicer with GrowCut, or a validated deep‑learning model). Define a training set for annotators, conduct a formal ICC analysis on ≥30 cases, and consider a consensus‐mask approach for the final dataset. |
| **Data Harmonisation** | Pre‑processing mentions resampling and intensity normalisation, but no discussion of scanner‑specific bias correction (e.g., ComBat). | Residual batch effects may inflate or deflate performance across sites. | Incorporate a harmonisation step (e.g., ComBat‑Gaussian) after feature extraction, and evaluate its impact on model stability. |
| **Class Imbalance** | High‑risk prevalence is likely <50 %; no plan for handling imbalance (oversampling, cost‑sensitive learning). | Model may be biased toward the majority class, reducing sensitivity. | Apply SMOTE, random undersampling, or use balanced‐loss functions during training; report sensitivity and specificity at clinically relevant thresholds. |
| **Outcome Definition** | The gold‑standard “high‑risk” label relies on INRG/COG criteria, which incorporate several clinical/pathologic factors. Some of these (e.g., MYCN status) may not be known at the time of the baseline CT. | Potential circularity: the model may be predicting a label that already includes imaging‑independent variables, limiting added value. | Clarify whether the model is intended to *replace* or *augment* the existing risk algorithm. Consider a secondary analysis using only variables available at imaging (e.g., stage, age) to isolate the pure imaging contribution. |
| **Prospective Validation Timeline** | A 24‑month enrolment window may be optimistic given neuroblastoma’s relative rarity (≈ 10‑15 new cases per centre per year). | Insufficient sample size for prospectively testing the AUC target. | Conduct a realistic accrual estimate per site; add additional centres or extend the enrolment period if needed. |
| **Regulatory Pathway** | No mention of intended regulatory classification (e.g., FDA SaMD) or pre‑market submission strategy. | Post‑validation implementation may stall without a clear pathway. | Outline early engagement with regulatory bodies (pre‑Submission meeting) and define the software as a Clinical Decision Support (CDS) tool subject to FDA‑2021 guidance. |
| **Statistical Plan Details** | Calibration methods are named, but no plan for recalibration (e.g., Platt scaling) if external validation shows mis‑calibration. | Decision‑curve analysis may be misleading if predicted probabilities are poorly calibrated. | Include a predefined recalibration step using the validation data and report both original and recalibrated performance. |
| **Health‑Economic Model Inputs** | Uses published cost data but does not specify source, perspective (payer vs. societal), or discount rate. | Results may be non‑transparent and not accepted by health‑technology assessment bodies. | Draft a full economic model protocol (Markov or decision tree) with sensitivity analyses on key cost and utility parameters. |
| **Data Governance** | Central data coordinating centre is mentioned, but no concrete data‑sharing agreement (DSA) or use of a Trusted Research Environment (TRE). | Potential legal barriers, especially for international sites. | Establish a DSA and host data in a certified TRE (e.g., UK NHS Safe Haven, US NCI Cancer Imaging Archive) with role‑based access. |
| **Risk Management** | No explicit risk‑mitigation table (e.g., for delayed site start‑up, scanner upgrades, loss of key personnel). | Project timelines could be jeopardised. | Create a simple RAID log (Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies) and assign owners. |
| **Patient/Parent Involvement** | No plan for patient‑focused outcomes, acceptability, or stakeholder engagement. | May affect uptake and funding justification. | Involve a patient advisory panel early to review consent forms, understand concerns about AI use, and co‑design the decision‑support interface. |

---

## Feasibility Verdict  

- **Technical Feasibility:** High. The imaging pipeline uses mature open‑source tools, and the required CT protocol (≤ 1.5 mm slices, arterial/venous phase) is already standard in paediatric oncology centres.  
- **Operational Feasibility:** Moderate. The retrospective component is realistic, but the prospective enrolment may fall short unless additional centres are recruited or the accrual period is extended.  
- **Regulatory Feasibility:** Adequate, provided that site‑specific IRB approvals and data‑transfer agreements are secured early. A pre‑market strategy should be incorporated if the final aim is a clinical‑decision tool.  
- **Statistical Feasibility:** Acceptable if a formal sample‑size calculation confirms ≥ 150‑200 high‑risk cases across all phases; otherwise the AUC CI may be too wide.  

---

## Recommendations for Strengthening the Protocol  

1. **Finalize the hypothesis and primary endpoint** in a single sentence and embed it in the abstract and study registration.  
2. **Perform a detailed sample‑size calculation** based on projected prevalence and desired AUC precision; present numbers for each phase.  
3. **Map all steps to workflow modules** (or create custom modules) to ensure end‑to‑end traceability in the audit system.  
4. **Standardize segmentation** with a defined software, training protocol, and ICC target; consider an automated deep‑learning segmenter to reduce manual workload.  
5. **Add a harmonisation step** (e.g., ComBat) and explicitly address class imbalance in model training.  
6. **Clarify the intended clinical role** of the radiomics signature (stand‑alone vs. additive) and design a secondary analysis that isolates the imaging contribution.  
7. **Re‑evaluate prospective accrual** – add 1–2 more sites or lengthen the enrolment window to guarantee ≥ 100 prospective cases.  
8. **Draft a regulatory pathway** (FDA SaMD, CE‑Mark) and plan a early engagement meeting.  
9. **Expand the health‑economic protocol** with perspective, discounting, and probabilistic sensitivity analysis.  
10. **Implement a robust data‑governance framework** (DSA, TRE) and a risk‑management log.  
11. **Involve patient/parent representatives** to ensure ethical acceptability and to shape the UI of the eventual decision‑support tool.  

---

### Bottom Line  

The study plan is comprehensive, methodologically sound, and aligns well with contemporary standards for AI/ML biomarker development in oncology. Addressing the gaps noted above—especially around hypothesis clarity, sample‑size justification, segmentation reproducibility, class imbalance, and prospective enrolment feasibility—will convert a strong proposal into a fully executable, high‑impact clinical research programme.
